node.label: Jack Goody
node.date_label: 1963 With Ian Watt, The Consequences of Literacy · 1983 The Development of the Family and Marriage in Europe · 2006 The Theft of History
node.description: Jack Goody brought anthropological comparison to histories of kinship, literacy and Eurasian societies. His jointly authored work with Ian Watt examined literacy; The Development of the Family and Marriage in Europe questioned claims about uniquely European family patterns while distinguishing kinship from demographic measures. The Theft of History criticizes accounts that make European experience the template for universal historical development. His comparisons seek similarities and differences across societies; they do not establish a single timeless family system or an undifferentiated East.
node.representative_figures_and_works: With Ian Watt, The Consequences of Literacy (1963); The Development of the Family and Marriage in Europe (1983); The Theft of History (2006).

proposed_edges.relationship: Questions the uniqueness and uniformity of European family patterns
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary 8–9 distinguishes kinship questions from demographic measures, stresses regional/social variation and considers Tibet/Roman Egypt counterexamples. The cited studies themselves were not independently checked.

proposed_edges.relationship: Challenges Europe-centred templates for world historical comparison
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Introduction 1–3 criticizes projecting European categories onto other societies and asks why Eurasian similarities disappear from divergence narratives. His argument is represented as a comparative challenge, not a proven global consensus.
